'''Otto Leiberich''' (5 December 1927 in [[Crailsheim]] - 23 June 2015) was a German [[Cryptography|cryptologist]] and [[mathematician]].<ref name="Laux2015">{{Citation |last=Laux |first=Hans |year=2015 |chapter=Otto Leiberich, Kryptomathematiker und Freund |title=Trilogie meines Lebens: Erinnerungen eines Aktuars |publisher=Verlag Versicherungswirtschaft |location=Karlsruhe |language=de |pages=128–136 |isbn=978-3-89952-902-9 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kWw1CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA130}}</ref><ref>{{DNB portal|105031399}}</ref> Leiberich is most notable for establishing the [[Federal Office for Information Security|Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik]] in 1991.<ref name="Hange-2015-OOL">{{Citation |last1=Hange |first1=Michael |title=Obituary for Dr Otto Leiberich | publisher=Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik|journal=Security in Focus – BSI Magazine 2015|volume=2015| date=15 December 2015 |pages=42–43 [22]|url=https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/Publications/Magazin/BSI-Magazin_2015.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=5#page=22 | access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref>

==Life==
Leiberich started his career during [[World War II]], conscripted as a soldier and working as a cryptanalyst in Chi IV of the [[Cipher Department of the High Command of the Wehrmacht|OKW/Chi]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Enigma Bulletin, Source:British Archives document:ADM 223/505|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D0QyAQAAIAAJ|access-date=13 June 2018|year=1997|publisher=Enigma Press|page=78}}</ref>

After studying mathematics and physics at the [[University of Cologne]], Leiberich earned a [[PhD#Germany|Dr.&nbsp;phil.]] in 1953 at the same university<ref>{{Citation |last=Laux |first=Hans |year=2015 | chapter=Otto Leiberich, Kryptomathematiker und Freund | title=Trilogie meines Lebens: Erinnerungen eines Aktuars | publisher=Verlag Versicherungswirtschaft | location=Karlsruhe |language=de | page=130 | isbn=978-3-89952-902-9 | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kWw1CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA130}}</ref> with a topic on algebra; his thesis ({{langx|de|"Über Systeme von Jardenschen Folgen"}}, On systems of Jarden sequences) was supervised by [[Guido Hoheisel]]. Leiberich joined the newly established post war German cipher bureau that from 1956 on was called the ''Central Cryptography Office''<ref name="Hange-2015-OOL"/> ({{langx|de|Zentralstelle für das Chiffrierwesen}} (ZfCh)). Dr [[Erich Hüttenhain]] was his director, both in OKW/Chi and in the new bureau.

==Career==
During the [[Cold War]] Leiberich and his team worked intensively on the [[cryptanalysis]] of double transposition ciphers. One of their results led in 1974 to the discovery of the spying activities of [[Günter Guillaume]] who was senior aide to [[Willy Brandt]], the statesman who served as [[Chancellor of Germany|Chancellor]] of the [[Federal Republic of Germany]] (West Germany) from 1969 to 1974.<ref name="Lasry2018">{{Citation |last= Lasry |first=George |year=2018 |title=A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics |publisher=kassel university press |location=Kassel | page=175 |isbn=978-3-7376-0458-1 |doi=10.19211/KUP9783737604598 |url=https://d-nb.info/1153797542/34
}}</ref> In 1972, Leiberich was the successor to [[Erich Hüttenhain]] as the Head of the Central Cryptography Office.<ref name="Bauer2006">{{cite book|author=Friedrich L. Bauer|title=Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hfWTDr_bvMwC&pg=PA415|access-date=12 June 2018|date=24 November 2006|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-48121-8|page=415}}</ref>

In 1999,  Leiberich wrote a report on the history of cryptography in Germany, which appeared in ''Spektrum der Wissenschaft'',<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leiberich |first1=Otto |title=Vom diplomatischen Code zur Falltürfunktion |journal=Spektrum der Wissenschaft |date=1 June 1999 |url=https://www.spektrum.de/magazin/vom-diplomatischen-code-zur-falltuerfunktion/825487 |access-date=13 June 2018 |publisher=Spektrum der Wissenschaft Verlagsgesellschaft mbH |language=de}}</ref> the German edition of the [[Scientific American]].

==Cipher challenge ==
In order to encourage research on the double [[transposition cipher]], Leiberich suggested during his retirement in 1999, that a double transposition challenge be published. Leiberich's recommendation for the challenge included:

* Both transposition keys should be long enough: 20 to 25 elements.
* The lengths of the ciphertext should not be a multiple of the length of either key. 
* A ciphertext of approximately 500 characters, i.e. the product of the lengths of the two keys, should be used.

These properties were based on Leiberich's own experience, designed with parameters to ensure its own security<ref name="Bauer2006"/> In 2007, the challenge was published by Klaus Schmeh,<ref name="Bauer2006"/> in various media channels including his own books, websites and academic and white papers.<ref name="Bauer2006"/>

In November 2013, [[George Lasry]], [[Nils Kopal]] and [[Arno Wacker]] solved the double transposition cipher using  a ciphertext only hill climbing attack. They also developed a [[Dictionary attack]] that also solved it.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lasry |first1=George |last2=Kopal |first2=Nils |last3=Wacker |first3=Arno |title=Solving the Double Transposition Challenge with a Divide-and-Conquer Approach |journal=Cryptologia |date=2014 |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=197–214 |doi=10.1080/01611194.2014.915269 |publisher=Taylor & Francis|s2cid=7946904 }}</ref>
